answers.explanation: No partitioning: whoever is sending gets the whole channel.
Collisions will happen, so the protocol is about noticing them and retrying well.
Only at the beginning of a slot. That's why the nodes must be synchronized.
The random choice is what breaks the tie between colliding nodes.
Randomness makes it likely that one node goes while the other waits.
Three S slots out of nine: the rest are collisions or empty.
1/e is about 0.37, so the channel is used for useful transmissions at most 37% of the time.
Maximizing Np(1-p)^(N-1) gives p = 1/N: on average one node tries per slot.
Pure ALOHA peaks at about 18%, half of slotted ALOHA's 37%, because frames can overlap partway through.
When only one node is busy, it gets every slot.
